touches.text: Ownership. The librarian owns every tree and delegates some to the devices that learn. EVERYTHING THAT LEARNS USING OUR GRAPH TREES IS A DELEGATE (CodeMother, chart and any learning block are examples, not a list), and each holds its trees by the librarian's delegation (Law 6: delegation through the owner's gate). WHY: two holders with different weights over the same nodes have different perspectives and can debate points, and the librarian, asked anything, can look at the query from both.

Delegation nests down the rungs: the librarian delegates a set of trees to a device, the device to its machines, a machine to its tools if one is ever that complex. Each stays co-owned by the one above. CodeMother's learning goes in her own tables, and she owns the learning blocks of her machines and tools.

The walk: a first HYPOTHESIS (0.7). CC's draft, written so the experiments (4.3.1.10) have something to be wrong about; it is replaced by what they show. WHY: Akien sets what the trees are for and judges what they do; the mechanism is the teammate's draft, the way the geogebra model was for the 3d scanner, and it is learned here by running it, not by specifying it first.

What a leaf weight is. Each node, in the tree's own leaf table, remembers the words that have led to it, with counts: "buffer" carries tank and cistern from plumbing, capacitor from electronics, inbox from mail, each with how often. This is where cross-domain comes from: the words of every field pile up on the same pattern node, so a new plumbing sentence reaches "buffer" by plumbing words and finds the electronics and the mail already there.

The walk. The string is cut into words deterministically (stems, no LLM). Start at the top; at each node score each child by how much of the string's words it has seen before, weighted by the counts; step to the best child; stop at a leaf, or when no child scores above the floor (a setting, measured). The result is the path taken, with each step's score.

The miss. A walk that cannot leave the top, or scores under the floor everywhere, cannot answer. Then, and only then, the LLM is asked, given the question, the string, and the tree's vocabulary at the node where it stopped: which of these answer it, or what new node belongs under this one? It returns names, existing or new, and nothing else, so the integration is plain code: a new node goes in the one list and under its parent; the string's words are added to the named nodes' counts. Then the walk runs again and lands. That is the learning: the next string like it needs no LLM.

The bench. The trees are learned by watching them run, so the first thing built on them is a way to see them: a graph-trees pane on the librarian's page (15) that draws a tree, takes a string and a question, lights the path with its scores, shows the embedding and the miss when there is one, and walks two strings from two domains side by side to see whether they land together; and the same from the command line, `cairn librarian walk "<string>" for <question>` (8.4.5). Every number in 4.3.1.9 (the floor, the buckets, the merge rule) is a setting, so an experiment is changing one and walking again. WHY: "i can imagine being able to understand it once i can run experiments and see what happens." Nothing in 4.3.1.9 is known until this has measured it (Law 3).

PURPOSE: The engine of a learning block: input -> candidates -> evaluate -> decide or escalate. In the walk's terms (4.3.1.9): decide is a walk that landed, and the deposit reinforces its path; escalate is a miss, first to the LLM (4.3.1.9.5), and when the LLM returns nothing usable, a question to the operator (17.19).

WHY: Many devices learn in the same shape; one engine, held by each, holding its trees by the librarian's delegation (4.3.1.4). "a learning block is a composite thing with many parts, it's a machine."

[Q#97: The first compile (ticket e889b197a3f6) turns a block's recorded runs into a deterministic floor. Which corpus should it learn from? Measured 2026-11-13: librarian-ask holds 7 engine runs. 4 are one question asked again, with the same winner every time; the other 3 are the host backfill, where every run escalated to you and carries_his_answer killed 5, 6 and 5 of 6 candidates. The engine traces give a floor that agrees with itself. The backfill kills give one that learns what your answers rule out. Should the first compile learn from the backfill (the kills), not the engine traces?]

conflicts.text: Each holder keeps its own data under ~/.cairn/devices/<holder>/<n>/machines/web_operator/. The librarian is the first holder (8.3.7).
conflicts.ticket_says: The floor berths in instance-space at ~/.cairn/devices/learning_block/0/floors/<block>.json
conflicts.why: Outline 16.4.3 specifies that shared machines' data is kept by each holder separately under ~/.cairn/devices/<holder>/<n>/machines/<machine>/ (the pattern used for web_operator). learning_block is a shared machine held by multiple devices (librarian, CodeMother, etc.), so it should follow the same pattern: each holder keeps its learning_block floors under its own instance directory, not at a top-level learning_block location
